the ground floor if they could have got that position. I may say that the revenue from the post office and customs amounts to about $13,000 a year.

I desire to congratulate the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) upon his elevation to the position of deputy Postmaster General. He tells us that he has recently aioopinted some person to the position of postmaster, and that he appointed a lawyer because he could not get any one better. Well, I myself would be at a loss to ascertain where you could get a better man than a lawyer. Doubtless since the hon. gentleman was promoted to the position of deputy Postmaster General he has been doing valiant service in several ridings, and he has left his trail in proof of his devotion to the present government. The Minister of Public Works says there is ground for congratulation in respect to the Clinton post office in the fact that the contract price of the building is only $9,500. The estimates so far show that we voted $7,500 last year, and we are asked to vote $8,000 additional this year, making $.15,500. Even if we stopped at this point I do not think there is ground for congratulation. The minister tells us that the total amount will be at least $18,000, and when we get this $18,000, I suppose, having regard to the history of the past, we will be requested to make a still further appropriation. So there is no reasonable hope that even $18,000 will finish the Clinton post office. There is no reason to believe that economy is being practised in this case, any more than in many other cases that have been before the committee. The hon. member for Halton tells us that he has been pressing the Minister of Public Works to do justice to the smaller towns and villages. There is every reason why this matter should be taken into consideration with a view of doing justice to the rural municipalities by giving them public buildings at a moderate cost. The suggestion made by my hon. friend from Halton that the residences of the postmasters should be combined with the post offices so as to dispense with the expense of caretakers, is, I think, a proper one.

Mr. Chairman, I think in this connection it would be fair to call the attention of the government to the policy of the Public Works Department in expending large sums of money in small towns just emerging from the condition of villages, on buildings altogether too_ ornate, too expensive for the purpose for which they are designed, and which, in fact, are more ornamental than useful. In this way a gross injustice is done to the agricultural portion of the community, many of whom have to travel two, three or four miles to get their mail matter when a large amount of expenditure is made in erecting these monumental
and expensive buildings in little towns, merely emerging from the state of village-hood. If favours are intended for towns of 2,000 or more, I put in a claim for a town in my own constituency, the town of Durham ; yet, I am strongly in favour of some move being made in the direction of the motion made by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) looking to the establishment of a rural mail delivery system. This, I believe, would probably be a very expensive undertaking and one that the department could not enter upon completely at the beginning; yet, some experimental steps might be taken in order to find out what the cost would be in extending it over the whole country. I believe that at any rate we should take some measures to show our disapprobation of the practice of erecting these costly structures, far more costly than the requirements warrant.

As I understand it, there was $5,000 voted for this building in the first place. Now, there is a contract let for $9,500 and the total cost will be about $18,000. Last year I drew the attention of the Department of Public Works to this kind of thing going on in respect to erecting public buildings. I asked then if there were any architects employed outside to prepare estimates, plans and specifications for these buildings. If there are surely the architect could come to some nearer figure than $5,000 or $6,000 for a building which we are subsequently told is going to cost $18,000. No private citizen would think of doing business in that way and no wonder that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House criticise items of this kind when they find these items growing to treble the amount at which they were placed when first introduced. I say it is high time that something should be done in the direction of putting a stop to this growing evil, for it is a growing evil. If the town of Clinton is entitled to a public building, one that will meet the requirements of the town, has not the department an architect who has brains enough to say whether a building proper for such a town shall cost $5,000 or $10,000 ? Instead of coming down with figures of this kind, the minister ought to be prepared to state exactly, or within a few hundred dollars, what a public building in a town of this kind should cost. I object very strongly to this kind of thing occurring year after year in this House. The time of this House'has been taken up in discussing items of this kind more than with the discussion of any other subject in the House. I am not blaming the hon. Minister of Public Works; this is an old, crying evil. He is not the father of this evil by any means, but I hope our good-natured minister will use his best efforts to have this kind of thing stopped and if he does I am sure he will deserve great credit and he will be commended on this side of the House.
Is this building intended for the joint purposes of the customs and post office, or the post office alone ?
It Is for the customs and the post office.
That is what the department paid for the site.

Then we have :
Weatherald, T., surveying, &e., $31.80.
. Who is that gentleman ?
He is the Conservative surveyor of the town of Goderich.
King's Printer, $09.08; advertising, $152 89 $221.97.
Does this amount of $69.08 mean paying for the advertising of this contract to the government Bureau, or to whom ?
It is the account of the King's Printer and it must have been for the plans and specifications.

Advertising, $152.89.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us what papers this advertisement appeared in ?
I have not the list of papers in which this contract was advertised.
Will the hon. minister bring it down ?
I will be very pleased indeed to bring it down.

Now, there is this account:
Travel of Ottawa officials : L. F. Taylor advanced ch. 960, $25.
Who is this gentleman ?
He is an architect in the department at Ottawa who went up to attend to this work ?

Legal expenses, James Scott, $34.
I suppose this is in connection with the plans, specifications, &c.
It is in connection with the transfer of the property.
Was there any local architect employed in Clinton ?
No, the work was all done in the department here.

Last year I brought up the question of architects in this House, and I find there are some ten architects engaged by the Public Works Department, or, at least, the Auditor General's report show's that number. I want to say to the hon. minister that this system of engaging architects in this country to look after public buildings is one that is not in the interest of the country. Last year I drew the attention of the department to it, quoting several buildings throughout the country where they paid large sums of money for clerks of works, to men who are architects residing in the localities in which public buildings are being built. The abuses that these men create in connection with the erection of these public buildings are simply these :	They are paid so much per day as
clerks of works, all the way from $2.50 to $7 a day and by reason of these architects receiving that amount of pay per day from one end of this country to the other the public buildings are being delayed in their construction. By reason of that payment by the day system, the work is extended for twice as long, yes, three times as long as it is necessary to construct these buildings. That abuse should be wiped out. It would pay the department better to have their own architects, or if they are obliged to engage outside architects to pay them on the principle of so much per cent on the contract price. Why, the way in which the armoury in my own city was constructed is a disgrace. They had two or three men, employed on that building months at a time, whereas if they were paying an architect by fees he would not have put up with the method of construction; he would make the contractors whoever they were put more men on the work so that it would be completed quicker, and there would be less money to be paid the architect. I am not going to find fault with the present Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) because he is a new man in the department, but I say that the system has been going on for years and it should be stopped.

So far as possible I have adopted the policy of making an arrangement with the local architect, as to what shall be charged by him for the building. I think the rule is a good one, that it will probably save a considerable amount of money, and that we may get better service. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) remembers as I do, the erection of the public building at St. Thomas which lasted for so many years, and in which they had a permanent caretaker. We have to take warning by the abuse in that case, and try to do a great deal better.

I have tried on some occasions to employ local men to prepare

plans but nearly in every case it was a failure. After six years of experience in tlie department I say that it is better that the plans should be prepared here in Ottawa. My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) must not lose sight of the fact that there is always a time limit fixed in the contract, so that the employment of a foreman to supervise the work at $2 or $3 a day cannot result in extending the time. I stated last year that it was not desirable to spend too large sums of money on public buildings and I am still of the same mind. At the same time we cannot forget that this country is growing pretty fast, that we are not building for one year or for two years, that we are putting up these buildings for at least fifty years. It would be imprudent and unwise not to look to the future. Might I suggest to the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) that if I was in his place, I would not be too much impressed by what is said in this House about the erection of these buildings-tempora mutantur, et nos mutamur in illis (times are changed and we are changed in them). If the minister will make a search in his department he will find hundreds of applications for public buildings. I was perhaps never able to gauge public opinion as my hon. friends on the other side have done, but I remember very well that for the past ten years complaint has been made in this House that we are not erecting enough public buildings, and the Public Works Department has had hundreds of petitions for public buildings from both sides of the House. If public opinion does not want public buildings, I verily believe that governments have not much interest in building them, because it is my experience that they give more trouble than power. The future of this country will be great; nobody can tell how many millions we will have in ten or twelve years. No one can say what the population of this town or that will be in ten years. I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works, that while remaining within the bounds of economy, he should not be too much impressed by criticisms which are indulged in by both sides of the House every time that a public building is erected.

I do not wish to unduly criticise the erection of public buildings, but I ask any member in this House if he were erecting a public building to cost $39,000, does he think it would take over a year to erect that building In my judgment it would not require more than six months, and that being so. what is the necessity of employing a clerk of works by the day at a large salary for so long a period as it now takes to erect these buildings.
If there wm no clerk of works, the building would not be satisfactory.
There slnu'd be a Vmit to the time.
It is necessary to have a good clerk of works and he should be there all the time or otherwise you will have botched work.
Was there a clerk of works employed on this building ?

Yes. I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) to say that where an arrangement could be made with the local architect he should get a percentage on the value of the work. I believe in that principle and I have done so in several cases lately. It would be a great mistake to let a contract and not have proper supervision on the work.
Who was the clerk of works here and how was he paid ?
His name was Henry Stevens and he was paid the usual fee of $3 a day-it was perhaps lower than the usual fee.
What is his usual occupation ?
Contractor and builder.

The linn, gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has told us that we do not know to what extent this country may grow, and that is the reason why I am so anxious that we should be economical and careful. I have been doing business in the province of Ontario for forty-five years and I can tell you that you would be very much surprised to find how very little most of these towns and villages have grown during the last twenty years. The population of these towns and villages is being depleted all the time on account of those who go not only from Ontario to the North-west, but also to the larger cities and towns. Concentration , is the order of business nowadays, not scattering. The policy of the present govern; ment seems to be to scatter their favours all over the country. I contend that it is bet-1 ter to concentrate, and that if a building is really required you should put up a good 1 building, but these small amounts you are spending through the villages of Canada are not justified by the requirements. I can tell , you that the post office and custom busi-t ness has been as well attended to in the past,
; as it will be in the future in these new , buildings. Because the Dominion of Can) ada is going to have an immense popula-t tion, is no reason why the little villages and , towns in Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario C should have buildings that will be an ex-i pense for all time, and the expense of which buildings will prevent you from developing in the right direction, namely, in the direc-. tion of our North-west and the larger towns c and cities.
A good deal has been said about a large amount of money being spent in Toronto. In consideration of the importance of Toronto as a commercial centre, I contend that

she has not had anything like the expenditure in proportion that many small villages have had. X have the greatest possible respect for the opinion, the energy and the courage of the late Minister of Public Works but I would not like to follow him in all matters of expenditure, not only on buildings, but on canals, railways, harbours and wharfs. We have spent an immense amount of money that is not productive and never will be, and I would urge the Minister of Public Works to be very careful how he allows himself to be pressed by his followers or any one else into large expenditures in the towns and villages throughout the province of Ontario. I am speaking as one who does business with them. I do not care about their politics or their votes. I am here only to speak as I feel and as my experience tells me is the right thing, regardless of the effect on politics or elections or anything of that kind; and I contend that if we spend hundreds and thousands of dollars in these ways in the province of Ontario, some day, when we pass off the crest of the wave, we shall be sorry for those expenditures and regret that we have not made them in some other direction. You will excuse me for extending my remarks to this length, but I do so because I feel anxious as a business man. I know that times are good and the government are getting more money than they expected; but I tell you that now is the time to be careful. It is not when times are hard and business is bad and money is scarce, but it is when money is plentiful, when people are filled up with ozone, that you ought to be careful, and that is why I warn you that you are making a mistake in moving in the direction that you are doing, and you will be making a greater mistake if you allow the late Minister of Public Works to urge you into expenditures that are not justifiable.

I do not mean that we should spend money without sense or reason, or erect buildings right and left without cause. But it seems to me that in government matters we should follow the same rules that are followed in ordinary business. The sense of the country to-day is that we should build well. My hon. friend in his own business has erected splendid buildings. This country is growing, and it seems to me that the government of the country should follow the course of ordinary business. I do not mean to say that we should spend money right and left, but I say that when we make up our minds to erect a pubile building, we should build it well. I do not mean to say anything more than that, and I believe that is a sound principle. My hon. friend has a great deal of confidence in this country. I have always found him to be a good patriot; he has always expressed himself in the House as a sound Canadian. I think I am not wrong in saying that in ten or twelve years we Mr. BROCK.
may have 10,000,000 people in Canada, and if we are going to grow in population as fast as we all hope, let us in our policy act accordingly.

I would like to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that I find a policy stated with a good deal of frankness on certain matters of this kind, in a journal which strongly supports the government, published in the town of Owen Sound. The editorial from which I will read was written with reference to the recent election which was in progress there. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works had much to do with that election; some other members of the cabinet were interesting themselves more actively in it. The paper gives some names, and perhaps I had better read them first;
The members of parliament who have taken part in this campaign so far for the Liberals are Colonel Thompson of Haldimand. C. B. Heyd of South Brant ; R. F. Sutherland of North Essex, and R. Holmes of West Huron, the latter being the only one remaining in the riding. Mr. Joseph Haycock, ex-M.P.P., of Frontenac, is also doing effective campaign work. On Tuesday evening, Hon. D. C. Fraser, the Guys-borough giant, and Dr. Macdonald, deputy speaker, will adress the electors of Owen Souud; other speakers are expected during the week.
I am glad to know that our honoured and respected Chairman was having so good a time on that occasion, in company with our hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Fraser).
Hon. Mr. Fielding will address a meeting here on Friday afternoon, which is intended to be for those who reside out of town, and will also address a meeting of the townspeople in the evening. It is expected that Hon. Mr. Muloek will also he in the riding next week.
That, however, Is only by the way. The doctrine of the government is stated here with a great deal of fulness and precision, and I am going to read it for the information of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, who has hardly expressed himself with considerable frankness but not with the brutal frankness of the writer of this editorial :
The country has never been more prosperous than it is at this moment under the able administration of tho Laurier government
Hear, bear.

Now, we shall see how much these hon, gentlemen will cheer something that follows, particularly the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes), who was so prominent in leading the cheering, and who took occasion to announce to the people very much the same doctrine as thst set forth in this Editorial ;
-and the to'Vn of Owen Sound never stood a better chavee of securing the expenditure of a large amount of money for the erection of public ouildings and for additional improvements in her harbour. These are considerations that invariably weigh well in a by-epetion, and. with ordinary care, should in-

sure the return of almost any candidate the party might choose to put in the field.
These, I suppose are the sentiments of the hon. member for West Huron.
Certainly.

X am glad that my hon. friend is equally frank with the editorial writer. Here are some further suggestions which I have no doubt equally commend themselves to my hon. friend's judgment :
This town is slated for certain favours within the gift of the government, and, to make a long story short, the electors cannot afford to kill their chances for securing them by electing an oppositionist.
That also, I take it, was the view my hon. friend from West Huron presented to the electors on that occasion; and possibly the fact that there was a certain disappointment in the result of that election may afford the reason why we do not observe the name of the town of Owen Sound in these estimates.
These are not all the estimates.
Oh, I see; my hon. friend proposes to put it in the supplementary estimates.
I advocated it some years ago, and I shall probably have to advocate it again if I hope to succeed.

That election was held some weeks ago, and my hon. friend has had time to consider the matter between the date of the election and the time when these estimates were brought down. If the reason I have suggested had nothing to do with the absence of the name of the town from the estimates, I cannot understand what the reason is.
These are not the right estimates.

The editor of this newspaper was evidently very high in the ranks of the Liberal party, he seeems to to have enjoyed the confidence of the leader of that party, because he seems to have known all about these gentlemen who were going to speak in the riding and the promises which they would hold out to the electors. Speaking seriously is it not a sad state of affairs that appropriations from the public revenue should be promised to or withheld from any constituency according as it returns a Liberal or Conservative candidate ? Is not that bribery pure and simple ? Is not that as direct an offer of a bribe to the voter as if yon offered him $5 for his vote ? The only difference is that in one case you are bribing the electors individually and in the other you are bribing them collectively. The hon.
member from West Huron (Mr. Holmes) is another of these gentlemen who addressed the constituents of North Grey on that occasion. He addressed the electors along those lines, and affirmed the principle in this House, when I read it to him from the newspaper to-night. If these hon. gentlemen can draw any distinction between bribing the electors individually and bribing them wholesale, let them draw it. The hon. member for West Huron speaking from his place has told us that these are proper appeals to be made to the electors and that these are proper considerations on which the electors should vote.

The hon. gentleman must not misrepresent my position. I was simply laughing and speaking in a bantering and jocular tone, and I do not think that the government should be held responsible for the editorial opinion of any newspaper.

Perhaps this may be a lesson to my hon. friend another time not to laugh too soon. I understood him to assert distinctly, though with a somewhat jeering smile, that that was exactly the kind of thing be believed in and that these were proper considerations to submit to the people. I am glad to know however that he did not believe what he said, or that he has concluded that the position he took is one which cannot be well defended. But it is not the first time that the constituency of North Grey has been treated to that sort of thing. When the Minister of Customs ran an election there some years ago, the people were invited to consider whether or not they would prefer that cold justice which they might expect if they elected the Conservative candidate or the warm sympathy to which they could look if they elected the Minister of Customs. It is not the first time in many ridings that that consideration has been put forward. It is very much in line with what seems to be the policy of the government as announced here to-night, and against that policy I raise my voice in protest and submit that there is not the slightest distinction between the offers of wholesale bribery of that kind and offers of individual bribery to the electors.

I see in one of the evening papers another evidence of this policy in North Ontario. The article is headed :-
DELIVERED GOODS, WANT THEIR PAY. Bracebridge Would Like Government to Fulfil North Ontario Election Promises.
Bracebridge has long been the principal point for a large summer resort territory in the Muskoka district, and is also in a constituency that lately turned down the ex-Minister of Finance and elected George D. Grant, a government supporter, and on both counts Bracebridge has something coming to her. A delegation from Bracebridge, composed of Mayor J. D. Shire, John Thompson, P. Hutchison, G. H. O. Thomas and H. J. Bird is registered at the Grand Union and is here to press the claims

of the town. They will see Sir William Mulock and Hon. Messrs. Sutherland and Paterson this afternoon and will ask for a new post office building.
I would like to ask the Hon. Minister of Public Works if it is his intention to grant that application.

I do not know what paper my hon. friend has quoted from, but every city is quite within its rights in sending a delegation to wait on any minister in order to press its claims. This deputation was not entirely composed of Liberals but of both Liberals and Conservatives. In the same way we have deputations from the city of Toronto to which we have given considerable time the last few days, and which are largely composed of very active Conservatives. As far as I am personally concerned I have always given all the time I could to receiving deputations, irrespective of politics. As regards Bracebridge, the question of giving that place a new post office was being negotiated before ever the election in North Ontario was thought of. Our late respected friend, Mr. McLeod, who supported the opposition and represented North Ontario, was pressing the claim of Bracebridge for a public building, and if the late member for Muskoka (Mr. O'Brien) were here, he would also say that that matter was engaging our attention while he was a member of this House and that it had nothing to do with the last election, or the election of the present representative. I also received a deputation headed by my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. McCormick) which was composed ol supporters of both parties, prominent merchants and manufacturers, and I am always pleased, when I think it is in the public interest, to grant public assistance from any of the departments irrespective of the political leanings of the hon. member who urges the claim. I remember that years ago, when the constituency which my hon. friend represents now was represented by Mr. Masson in this House, I, in my humble way, tried to impress the late government with the desirability of recognizing the claim he was making for a building at that time. AVhile I am not prepared to say that all things being equal, the government would not be more influenced by their supporters than by their opponents, I for one will always ask the House to vote such expenditures solely in the public interest. If more of these votes are for constituencies represented by Liberals during many years in this House than for those represented by Conservatives, it is simply because, under the policy which was carried out by the late government, the majority of constituencies represented by Conservatives do not require public buildings. For many years the late government carried out the policy of refusing any consideration, except in extreme cases, to constituencies represented by Liberals. I for Mr. REID (Grenville).
my part am not disposed to adopt any such policy. I think that the less partisanship you have in these matters the better and that in every case fair consideration should be given on its merits to the demand of any constituency.

It is refreshing to hear the hon. leader of the opposition talking about the government trying to bribe constituencies in a wholesale manner. But let me draw his attention to the fact that for eighteen years the party he leads resorted to that policy. I remember that in my constituency they went so far as to promise a mounted police barracks to a certain portion of that constituency if the government candidate were elected, and to show their bona fides they hauled a lot of sand on to the ground and got the surveyor to lay out the location. But after the election the stone and sand were hauled away and nothing more was done. On another occasion not only did their newspapers publish articles, but their candidate himself told the people plainly that if they voted for the government they would get a barracks worth $60,000 to $70,000. The government candidate was elected and the people got the barracks. I remember that on the occasion of another election we had in my constituency, the members of the mounted police were promised scrip and medals if they would vote for the Conservative candidate. They were paraded by their officers in the barracks square and telegrams were read from the Conservative government to the effect that if they voted for the Conservative candidate they would get the scrip and medals. They voted, but they have never received the scrip or medals to this day. That sort of thing was carried on throughout the Northwest. One candidate used to say : What is the use of voting for an opposition candidate ?-you can't get anything for your riding; if you want improvement or public buildings, or more police, vote for me. It is amusing to find a gentleman rising here talking economy, when I understand that it is only two weeks since that hon. gentleman headed a delegation to the Minister of Public Works asking for a grant of $250,000 to spend in the city of Toronto.
What for.

It makes no difference what it was for. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) headed a delegation asking for that expenditure in the city. Now he says it is not right for the government to spend a certain amount in the small towns in Ontario, because they are at a standstill or going back. But I think the small towns have as good a right to have public moneys spent in them as the larger cities have. They are contributing to the revenues, and I do not see why they have not the right to get the benefit of some of the expenditure. It is Just as necessary to have a post office in a small town as in a big one.

I hope that the Minister of Public Works will continue to look after the interests of the smaller communities as well as of the larger ones that can have a delegation wait upon the minister headed by influential members of the House of Commons.

I do not think that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) does justice to the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). That gentleman did hold out inducements-a post office, dry dock and other public works-to the electors to support the Liberal candidate. But he made amends for it on the following Sunday, when he lectured in the Young-Men's Christian Association and I understand his subject was, ' The Right Road to Heaven.' I am glad to hear the hon. Minister of Public Works say the fact that North Grey had elected a member in opposition to the government would not interfere with the department spending money in public works there. The government derive a large revenue from the town of Owen Sound. We have no public building. I believe it would be in the interests of the country, even as a matter of economy, to erect a public building there. I asked the hon. minister last night if he would let us know the amount expended by the government for rent in Owen Sound. It was a very considerable sum, and I believe that if it were capitalized it would pay for the erection of a splendid building. Therefore, r hope the hon. minister will not refuse to consider the erection of a building because the riding has sent a representative in opposition to the government.
The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) attacked me just now, stating that I had headed a deputation that asked the government for the expenditure of $250,000 in Toronto. In the first place-
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) wishes to criticise anything I have said-

No, I am criticising what the hon. member for Saskatchewan said. He told us how extravagant the late government were and how wrong the expenditure of public money in his constituency had been and stated that I had called upon the hon. minister at the head of a deputation to ask for the expenditure of $250,000 in Toronto. If the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Davis') other statements about drawing stone and leaving sand and so on, in his constituency, were exaggerated to the same extent as his statements about me, he has not added much strength to the government's case. I can assure the hon. gentleman that what he has stated as to my demands on the government on behalf of the city of Toronto is ridiculously exaggerated.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) a question :	Does
he mean to say that he did not attend with the delegation that waited upon the Minister of Public Works to ask for the expenditure of an amount of public money on Toronto ?

Most assuredly I say so. Either the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) was misinformed or else he is wilfully stating what is untrue. I was one of a deputation that called upon the minister to ask him for $50,000 for the Dominion exhibition, which $50,000 was to be expended largely for the country from which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) comes, in paying freight on cattle and other products from there to be exhibited.

I am credibly informed, and I think I am right, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) was with a delegation that asked for $250,000 which, if not to spend in the city of Toronto, was to be spent on Toronto harbour improvements. Was that not the same thing ?
I say I was with no such delegation.
I hope, then, that we may conclude that the hon. gentleman does not approve of that expenditure of $250,000.

It seems to me that the Minister of Public Woi'ks had to go far afield to find an argument to justify some of these items when he brought up the fact that a delegation had waited upon him a few days ago asking for an expenditure on behalf of the city of Toronto.
That was the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis).

No, the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) made that statement in the early part of the evening. The hon. member for Saskatchewan was not in his place. But that makes no difference. If the Minister of Public Works had been as frank as we have generally found him in making explanations to this House, he might have explained for what purpose the sums asked for were required. A committee, nonpolitical in its character, and headed by the mayor of Toronto, who is a Liberal, came to ask for a grant in aid of the Dominion exhibition. He was supported by gentlemen, a large number of whom are supporters of the government and on the directorate of that exhibition. And what was it they asked for ? I think hon. members will agree that the Toronto Industrial Fair offers the best opportunity that is afforded, from one end of Canada to the other, and year after year, for those who are producers, to exhibit their products to the best advantage. For the last twenty-five years the Toronto exhibition has done a great work, whose benefits have not been confined to Toronto or Ontario, but have been as wide as the Dominion. The splendid pto-, gress which ha s been made by the Domin-

My hon. friend reads me a strong lesson, but he is proceeding on a wrong basis. If he had been in the House and had heard what was said previously, he would not have given me the scolding we have just heard. My hon. friend from Centre Toronto asked me a question as to whether an application had been made by the citizens of Clinton for the grant that was being considered. I thought he was very unfairly criticising the vote and the action of these people in asking for this grant, and it was in that connection that I said that the people from other constituencies had just as much right to wait upon the members of the government and to present their claims as had the deputation from Toronto. I do not think my hon. friend need be quite so thin skinned about it. He knows that I have always lent my assistance to him when I thought his appeals were in the public interest. I do not think Toronto is neglected. I did not mean to be offensive in giving my answer, or in making that re-

mark in replying to his colleague in regard to the particular vote that was then under consideration. As I said, last year a deputation headed by the late member waited upon the government stating that they were entitled to consideration. I had no intention of reflecting on my hon. friend in any respect whatever. X said that every citizen was within his right in making an application and supporting it by the assistance of other citizens of the town in question. If my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) criticises us very unfairly and unjustly on some votes made for outside constituencies, he must not get so hot if we take our own time. We are within our rights as long as we are not offensive in our language, and as long as we do it in a parliamentary manner, the hon. gentleman must not get cross and scold. I have recognized the importance of the city of Toronto as well as he has done ; I think he has always found me an active supporter of the institutions and of the commercial and business interests of that city, and I have done everything that I could to advance its progress. I propose to do so in a public way in future, notwithstanding the attack made upon me by my hon. friend. I suppose that the reason I am called upon to defend myself is that he was very much in earnest in opposing this vote, and thought that the town of Clinton should not have the same consideration as a large city.

I would be sorry to get the reputation of being a scold. I appeal to the records to show that I have not taken up the time of the House in criticising harshly or adversly the votes asked by the government. What I objected to was that occasion should be taken by the hon. gentleman of this vote to Clinton to drag in Toronto. I spoke with the greatest possible respect of the ministers of the Crown. I said, and I say still, that I think the Minister of Public Works should have been franker in his treatment of the reasonable request made by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) in asking upon what principle these grants were made.

He asked a question as to what particular vote I supported. Other representations were made to me by the deputation. If the hon. gentleman had been attending to the wants of the city of Toronto he would know that they asked for three more public buildings.

I was quite aware that it was the intention of the hon. Postmaster General to ask that three branch post offices be erected. I heard what the hon. Postmaster General had to say. The hon. Postmaster General was not in his place or we might have criticised the wisdom of establishing these branches rather than providing a central post office near the railway station. I took the opportunity a few years
ago of making a statement in the House to the effect that notwithstanding the technical knowledge that the hon. Postmaster General has acquired since he has been at the head of the Post Office Department the public interest and the interests of the people would be better served if there was a central post office near the chief railway station than by establishing branch post offices. I paid a great deal of attention to what the hon. gentleman had to say when making reply to the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), and I expressed regret that he was not in his seat at the time when these appropriations were asked for. The hon. gentleman has admitted very frankly that the appropriations asked for by the deputation from Toronto are appropriations in the general interest. I may say that the city of Toronto only asks what it believes itself to be entitled to, and that in making the request that is made on this occasion it is merely asking that the public generally shall be enabled to reap a greater advantage than they have reaped in the past from the industrial exhibition.
The people of Clinton think the same in regard to their appropriation.

I was going to say so far as the appropriation of $50,000 asked for the industrial exhibition is concerned, the object for which it is asked is one that commends itself to the wisdom of this House. And, as far as the $200,000 is concerned, we are merely asking that tardy justice be done for the injury that has been wrought to the city of Toronto in the past, for the injury that has been done the Toronto harbour through the action of the government in days gone by. We are asking that the harbour should be put in first class condition and we believe that if this were done a substantial advantage would be given, not only to the people of Ontario, but to the people east and west of the city of Toronto by reason of the greater facilities for the shipment of different kinds of commodities.
I should like to say a word in reference to the complaint made by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is all out of order. Hon. gentlemen are discussing questions absolutely and entirely irrelevant to the item under consideration.
The hon. gentleman put me in a false position. The hon. gentleman tried to make it appear that-
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) has a right to answer the hon. member for West Toronto.

The hon. gentleman made the insinuation when he was on his feet that I was opposing a certain grant of money that was made for the harbour of Toronto

and he said that the harbour of Toronto was a harbour that was being improved in the interest of the whole country. X did not intend nor do I intend to oppose any expenditure of money on the harbour of Toronto, but I was merely pointing out that if the people of Toronto wanted money spent in their own town they should not be so small as to object to the amounts of money being spent in the smaller towns and in rural districts.

X asked the hon. minister about the parties the department bought this lot from and I quoted :
Potter, F. A.. Potter, D. and Moore, T., executors estate of late Ann Moore, purchase of site, $2,500.
The hon. gentleman said that they bought this site from these people. Is that correct ?
My information is that this property was owned by the executors of an estate. There is no doubt about that, because the hon. gentleman has read the names of the excu-tors.
Who is the party that the lot was bought from ?
It is an estate known in Clinton as the Potter estate.
Is there any name that the hon. gentleman could give us ?
You have the names there.

That is what I cannot understand. Last year, we were not told that; we were told an entirely different story. We were told last year that the lot had been purchased from Mr. A. W. Wilkie, who happened to be a good Tory.
Mr. Wilkie was simply the tenant of the property. The property was bought from the Potter estate.

All I have to do is to quote the Minister of Public Works :
We have bought the site there from a good opponent of ours, Mr. A. W. Wilkie. We will spend more than $8,000 on the building.
Which statement is correct ? Iam bound to believe that of the hon. member for West Huron, in view of the fact that he displayed such a Christian spirit at the Sunday school convention recently held in Owen Sound during the late election there. I am bound to say also that we have a good running mate for the hon. member for West Huron, in Preston, the gentleman who sang at a meeting of Sunday School children in St. Thomas, during the famous corrupt election in West Elgin. 'There is Sunshine in my Soul.' I would like to put these two gentlemen together as they make an excellent team.
Cobourg-Towards construction of armoury, .5,000.
I do not suppose we will be called upon to sit all night.
Perhaps it is a little unreasonable to sit here wasting time altogether. If my hon. friend has any proposition in regard to these items we may arrange to adjourn.

Of course I sympathize with my hon. friend in the obstruction he has sustained on his own side of the House, but, we are not responsible for that. The suggestion I was going to make was that as we have made pretty fair progress with these three items, and as we have discussed some of these matters pretty fully, which no doubt will save discussion on similar items in future, we should now rise and report progress.
Allow the present item to be passed and we will agree to adjourn.
We will allow that item to pass on the understanding which I have with the minister that if any lion, gentleman who is not here wishes to discuss it he may do so on some other item.
Perhaps the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) will give us some explanation about that Sunday convention.
I will if the hon. member for Victoria (Mi-. Hughes) will tell us something about limelight views in North Ontario.
I accept the hon. gentleman's challenge and on a later occasion will throw some limelight views on his actions there.

I am afraid we will not have to call the hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) to account for doing much Sunday school work.
I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Thubsdat, March 26, 1903.
